nameStory: This moss is named after Swedish botanist Göran Wahlenberg (1780-1851), who explored the Arctic regions of Scandinavia and described many northern plant species. The 'spur' part of the name refers to the small, pointed projections on the moss capsules that help distinguish this species from its relatives.
description: Wahlenberg's Spur Moss is a tiny, cushion-forming moss that creates small, dense patches on rocks and soil. The individual plants are only about 5-10 millimeters tall, forming compact green cushions that might be easily overlooked without close inspection. When dry, the moss appears grayish-green and somewhat shriveled, but it transforms into a brighter green when moistened. This is an uncommon moss in New England, found in just a few specialized habitats.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, tight cushions or low mats, typically 1-2 inches across, with individual shoots packed closely together like tiny green pins in a pincushion

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that curve inward when dry, giving the moss a twisted appearance; under a hand lens, leaves have a single central vein (midrib)

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Small, cylindrical capsules on short stalks with distinctive tiny spurs or teeth around the opening; capsules are reddish-brown when mature

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dull grayish-green when dry, brightening to yellow-green or bright green when wet; older parts may appear brownish

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on acidic rocks, thin soil over bedrock, and occasionally on sandy or gravelly substrates in exposed locations

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and crispy when dry, becoming soft and slightly springy when moist; cushions are firm and compact to the touch

habitat: This rare moss typically grows on exposed acidic rocks, thin soils over granite or other acidic bedrock, and occasionally on sandy banks. In New England, it's most likely to be found in mountainous areas or exposed ledges where few other plants can survive. Look for it in areas with good air circulation and minimal competition from larger plants.

seasonality.spring: Moss begins to green up with increased moisture, and sporophytes (if present) may be developing. This is often the best time to spot the bright green coloration.
seasonality.summer: Mature sporophytes may be present with their distinctive spurred capsules. The moss may appear more grayish during dry spells but quickly greens up after rain.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes release spores and begin to deteriorate. The moss remains visible but may be less vibrant as moisture levels fluctuate.
seasonality.winter: Moss persists through winter, though it may be less noticeable under snow. During mild, wet periods, it can still show green coloration.

funFact: This tiny moss is so rare in New England that it has only been documented twice in the entire region, making it one of our most elusive bryophytes - you're more likely to spot a rare orchid than this diminutive cushion moss!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small, cushion-forming mosses like Grimmia species, but Wahlenberg's Spur Moss has the distinctive spurred capsules (when present) and typically grows in more acidic conditions. Remember: spurred capsules are the smoking gun for identification.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it might be related to other 'spur' plants, the moss world uses different naming conventions than flowering plants. The 'spur' here refers specifically to tiny projections on the spore capsules, not to any flower-like structures.
compareHints: Since this is the only Brideliella species in our region, compare it with other small cushion mosses in the broader Rhabdoweisiaceae family, which tend to grow in similar rocky, acidic habitats. The key difference is the spurred capsule opening, which is unique among our regional species. Most other cushion mosses in similar habitats lack these distinctive capsule features.
